prompt: With `c3` stopped, two writes at `QUORUM` succeed. What does the coordinator `c1` do about `c3`'s copy?

choices.text: Keeps them as hints, to replay for c3
choices.why: Right: a file in c1's hints directory, replayed and deleted once c3 was back.

choices.text: Nothing; c3 gets the data at the next repair only
choices.why: Repair would fix it too, but hints come first and cost less.

choices.text: Refuses the writes until c3 is back
choices.why: QUORUM needs two of three, and had them.

choices.text: Writes c3's copy to c2 instead, permanently
choices.why: Placement never changes because a node is down.

prompt: The hint file on `c1` was named `1fe37605-9cd6-…-2.hints`. What did the first part of the name identify?

choices.text: The table the writes belonged to
choices.why: Hints are kept per target node, not per table.

choices.text: The coordinator that stored the hint
choices.why: The file is on the coordinator already; the name says whom it is for.

choices.text: A checksum of the two updates
choices.why: It matched the host ID in nodetool status.

choices.text: c3's host ID
choices.why: Right: the same ID nodetool status showed on the DN line.

prompt: `nodetool getmaxhintwindow` printed `10800000 ms`. How many hours is that?
While the hint file was in the directory, `nodetool listpendinghints` said there were none. What does the lesson take from that?

choices.text: The hints had already been delivered to c3
choices.why: c3 was stopped; the log line about delivery came after it started.

choices.text: Trust the directory, not the tool
choices.why: Right. A tool that says nothing is easy to believe during an incident.

choices.text: Hinted handoff was switched off on c1
choices.why: statushandoff said it was running, and the file was written and replayed.

choices.text: The file was a leftover from an earlier run
choices.why: It carried c3's host ID and was replayed when c3 returned.

prompt: In which of these cases does a replica end up behind with no hint to fix it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The node was down for five hours, with the default window
choices.why: Right: past three hours no hints are kept.

choices.text: The node was down for ten minutes
choices.why: Well inside the window; its hints replay.

choices.text: The coordinator holding the hints was lost too
choices.why: Right: the hints lived on it.

choices.text: A live replica dropped a write under load
choices.why: Right: it was never marked down.

choices.text: The write was at ALL
choices.why: A write at ALL fails with a node down, so there is nothing to hint.

prompt: In the traced read at `ALL`, the coordinator asked `c3` for data and `c2` for a digest. What is a digest?

choices.text: The commit log entries for the row
choices.why: The commit log is never sent to answer a read.

choices.text: A summary of the replica's SSTables
choices.why: It is about one query's answer, not the files.

choices.text: The replica's Merkle tree for the range
choices.why: Merkle trees belong to repair, not to reads.

choices.text: A hash of the replica's answer, sent instead of the data
choices.why: Right. Equal digests mean equal answers; a mismatch triggers the full read.

prompt: After `Digest mismatch`, what did the client receive, and what happened to `c3`?

choices.text: An error, and c3 was marked down
choices.why: The read succeeded; a mismatch is repaired, not reported.

choices.text: The value 5 from c3, which then sent it to the others
choices.why: The newest value wins, and that was 4.

choices.text: The value 4, and c3 received a read-repair mutation
choices.why: Right: READ_REPAIR_RSP came back from c3.

choices.text: Both values, for the application to choose
choices.why: Cassandra resolves by timestamp and returns one value.

prompt: A row was deleted while one replica was down, and nobody ever reads that row again. Will read repair ever fix the stale replica?

choices.text: Yes, at the next compaction
choices.why: Compaction is local and compares nothing between replicas.

choices.text: No: only rows that are read ever get fixed by it
choices.why: Right. That is why repair exists, and why deletes depend on it.

choices.text: Yes, because read repair also runs in the background every hour
choices.why: There is no background read repair in 5.0; read_repair_chance was removed in 4.0.

choices.text: No, because deletes are never read-repaired
choices.why: A tombstone is read-repaired like any value, when a read compares replicas.

prompt: The table setting that makes the client wait until a read repair is written has the value ___.
Why does repair build Merkle trees instead of sending every row to compare?

choices.text: Only Merkle trees carry tombstones
choices.why: Tombstones are streamed like any data.

choices.text: Merkle trees take up less space on disk than the SSTables do
choices.why: They are built in memory for the repair, not stored as data.

choices.text: Trees let repair skip reading the data
choices.why: Building the tree reads the data: that is the validation compaction.

choices.text: Equal hashes settle whole slices without sending them
choices.why: Right. The comparison costs hashes, and the streaming costs only the differences.

prompt: The full repair of `shop` reported `orders_by_customer` out of sync on every pair of nodes, though no node had been down while it was written. Why?

choices.text: Hinted handoff had replayed the orders twice
choices.why: A duplicate write is idempotent and leaves hashes equal.

choices.text: Its SAI index had diverged between nodes
choices.why: This lesson's staged table has no index; the difference is the rows.

choices.text: The ALTER raised copies to three and moved none of the old rows
choices.why: Right. This was the repair lesson 17's warning asked for.

choices.text: Clustering order differs per node
choices.why: It is part of the schema, the same everywhere.

prompt: After an incremental repair, `tablestats` showed `Percent repaired: 100.0`. What does the next incremental repair of that table read?

choices.text: Every SSTable again, since repaired data is compared too
choices.why: That is a full repair; the incremental one skips stamped SSTables.

choices.text: Only SSTables without a Repaired at stamp, written since
choices.why: Right. That is the saving, and also why a full repair is still run now and then.

choices.text: Nothing, until gc_grace_seconds expires
choices.why: Incremental repair has no such wait.

choices.text: The commit log of each replica
choices.why: Repair works on SSTables, never on the commit log.

prompt: Match each line from the repair log to what it meant.

pairs.right: the coordinator asked each replica to hash its range
two pairs of replicas disagreed and must exchange data
the table's replicas agree after the repair

prompt: Put the steps of a repair session in order.
items: Ask every replica for a Merkle tree of the range
Each replica reads its data and builds the tree
Compare the trees and create sync tasks for differing slices
Stream the differing slices between replicas

prompt: A table's `gc_grace_seconds` is 432000. Within how many days must every replica be repaired?
Why does a schedule usually run `nodetool repair -pr` on every node rather than plain `nodetool repair`?

choices.text: -pr is the only form that repairs tombstones
choices.why: Both forms carry tombstones; -pr is about how much work is repeated.

choices.text: -pr covers each range once
choices.why: Right. With three copies that is a third of the work.

choices.text: -pr runs without reading data
choices.why: It still builds Merkle trees from the data.

choices.text: Plain repair is refused on more than one node
choices.why: It runs; it repeats work.

prompt: Repair has silently failed for three weeks and someone finally fixes the job. What does the lesson say to expect from its first successful run?

choices.text: Deleted rows coming back, copied from stale replicas
choices.why: Right. The cost of a stopped repair is paid on the day it is fixed.

choices.text: A quick run, since there has been little to repair
choices.why: Three weeks of drift is more work, not less.

choices.text: A refusal, because repair cannot run after gc_grace_seconds
choices.why: Repair runs at any time; it just cannot restore purged tombstones.

choices.text: Lost writes, since repair keeps the oldest version
choices.why: Repair keeps the newest timestamp.

prompt: What should a repair alert watch, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Only repair commands that end with an error
choices.why: A repair that never starts never errors.

choices.text: The read repair count of the busiest table
choices.why: Read repair covers only what is read.

choices.text: The number of hint files on each coordinator
choices.why: Hints say a node is down, not that repair has run.

choices.text: The age of each node's last good repair
choices.why: Right. It fires for a job that broke as well as one that fails.

prompt: Match each mechanism to what it misses.

pairs.right: a node down longer than max_hint_window
nothing, if it runs within gc_grace_seconds

prompt: A team's cluster has never run repair, and reads at `QUORUM` have always looked right. Which statement fits this lesson?

choices.text: Correct QUORUM reads prove the replicas agree
choices.why: Read repair fixes what is read; unread rows and stale copies stay behind.

choices.text: Some deletes are now beyond repair
choices.why: Right. The first repair they run could bring some of them back.

choices.text: Hints have kept every replica up to date
choices.why: Hints have limits, and a live replica that dropped a write never gets one.

choices.text: Incremental repair runs on its own by default
choices.why: The 5.0.9 node logged that auto-repair is disabled.
